questions.prompt: Which identity is useful for reducing \(\sin^2 x\) in an even-power integral?
questions.answer:
Use the half-angle identity
\[\boxed{\sin^2 x=\frac{1-\cos 2x}{2}}.\]
It changes an even power into an expression that can be integrated directly.

questions.prompt: Which identity rewrites \(\tan^2 x\) in terms of \(\sec^2 x\)?
questions.answer:
Use
\[\boxed{\tan^2 x=\sec^2 x-1}.\]
This is useful because \(\int \sec^2 x\,dx=\tan x+C\).

Since \(\frac{d}{dx}\cos x=-\sin x\),
\[\int \sin x\,dx=\boxed{-\cos x+C}.\]

The derivative of \(\tan x\) is \(\sec^2 x\). Therefore
\[\boxed{\int \sec^2 x\,dx=\tan x+C}.\]

Use
\[\cos^2 x=\frac{1+\cos 2x}{2}.\]
Then
\[\int \cos^2 x\,dx=\frac12\int(1+\cos2x)dx.\]
So
\[\boxed{\frac{x}{2}+\frac{\sin2x}{4}+C}.\]

Use
\[\sin^2 x=\frac{1-\cos2x}{2}.\]
Then
\[\int \sin^2x\,dx=\frac12\int(1-\cos2x)dx.\]
Therefore
\[\boxed{\frac{x}{2}-\frac{\sin2x}{4}+C}.\]

Separate one \(\sin x\):
\[\sin^3x=(1-\cos^2x)\sin x.\]
Let \(u=\cos x\), so \(du=-\sin x\,dx\). Then
\[\int \sin^3x\,dx=-\int(1-u^2)du.\]
So
\[\boxed{-\cos x+\frac{\cos^3x}{3}+C}.\]

Separate one \(\cos x\):
\[\cos^3x=(1-\sin^2x)\cos x.\]
Let \(u=\sin x\), so \(du=\cos x\,dx\). Then
\[\int \cos^3x\,dx=\int(1-u^2)du.\]
Thus
\[\boxed{\sin x-\frac{\sin^3x}{3}+C}.\]

Use
\[\tan^2x=\sec^2x-1.\]
Then
\[\int \tan^2x\,dx=\int(\sec^2x-1)dx.\]
Therefore
\[\boxed{\tan x-x+C}.\]

Let \(u=\sin x\), so \(du=\cos x\,dx\).
Then
\[\int \sin^2x\cos x\,dx=\int u^2\,du=\frac{u^3}{3}+C.\]
Thus
\[\boxed{\frac{\sin^3x}{3}+C}.\]

Because the sine power is odd, save one \(\sin x\):
\[\sin^3x\cos^2x=(1-\cos^2x)\cos^2x\sin x.\]
Let \(u=\cos x\), so \(du=-\sin x\,dx\).
Then
\[-\int(1-u^2)u^2du=-\int(u^2-u^4)du.\]
So
\[\boxed{-\frac{\cos^3x}{3}+\frac{\cos^5x}{5}+C}.\]

Because the cosine power is odd, save one \(\cos x\):
\[\sin^2x\cos^3x=\sin^2x(1-\sin^2x)\cos x.\]
Let \(u=\sin x\), so \(du=\cos x\,dx\).
Then
\[\int u^2(1-u^2)du=\int(u^2-u^4)du.\]
Thus
\[\boxed{\frac{\sin^3x}{3}-\frac{\sin^5x}{5}+C}.\]

Use \(\sin^2x=\frac{1-\cos2x}{2}\):
\[\sin^4x=\left(\frac{1-\cos2x}{2}\right)^2=\frac{1-2\cos2x+\cos^2 2x}{4}.\]
Use \(\cos^2 2x=\frac{1+\cos4x}{2}\):
\[\sin^4x=\frac38-\frac12\cos2x+\frac18\cos4x.\]
Integrate:
\[\boxed{\frac{3x}{8}-\frac{\sin2x}{4}+\frac{\sin4x}{32}+C}.\]

Use \(\cos^2x=\frac{1+\cos2x}{2}\):
\[\cos^4x=\left(\frac{1+\cos2x}{2}\right)^2=\frac{1+2\cos2x+\cos^2 2x}{4}.\]
Since \(\cos^2 2x=\frac{1+\cos4x}{2}\),
\[\cos^4x=\frac38+\frac12\cos2x+\frac18\cos4x.\]
Therefore
\[\boxed{\frac{3x}{8}+\frac{\sin2x}{4}+\frac{\sin4x}{32}+C}.\]

Rewrite
\[\tan^3x=\tan x(\sec^2x-1).\]
Then
\[\int \tan^3x\,dx=\int \tan x\sec^2x\,dx-\int\tan x\,dx.\]
For the first integral, let \(u=\tan x\), giving \(\frac12\tan^2x\). Also \(\int\tan x\,dx=\ln|\sec x|\).
Thus
\[\boxed{\frac12\tan^2x-\ln|\sec x|+C}.\]

Save \(\sec^2x\) and rewrite the rest:
\[\sec^4x=\sec^2x\sec^2x=(1+\tan^2x)\sec^2x.\]
Let \(u=\tan x\), so \(du=\sec^2x\,dx\).
Then
\[\int \sec^4x\,dx=\int(1+u^2)du=u+\frac{u^3}{3}+C.\]
Therefore
\[\boxed{\tan x+\frac{\tan^3x}{3}+C}.\]

Save one sine factor:
\[\sin^5x=(1-\cos^2x)^2\sin x.\]
Let \(u=\cos x\), so \(du=-\sin x\,dx\).
Then
\[-\int(1-u^2)^2du=-\int(1-2u^2+u^4)du.\]
Integrate:
\[-u+\frac{2u^3}{3}-\frac{u^5}{5}+C.\]
Thus
\[\boxed{-\cos x+\frac{2\cos^3x}{3}-\frac{\cos^5x}{5}+C}.\]

questions.prompt: A student says \(\int \sin^2x\,dx=\frac{\sin^3x}{3}+C\). Diagnose the error and give the correct answer.
questions.answer:
The formula \(\frac{\sin^3x}{3}\) would differentiate to \(\sin^2x\cos x\), not \(\sin^2x\). The missing \(\cos x\) factor means direct substitution \(u=\sin x\) is not valid.
Use the half-angle identity:
\[\sin^2x=\frac{1-\cos2x}{2}.\]
Then
\[\int\sin^2x\,dx=\frac12\int(1-\cos2x)dx=\boxed{\frac{x}{2}-\frac{\sin2x}{4}+C}.\]

questions.prompt: Derive a reduction formula for \(I_n=\int \sin^n x\,dx\) for \(n>1\).
questions.answer:
Write
\[I_n=\int \sin^{n-1}x\sin x\,dx.\]
Use integration by parts with \(u=\sin^{n-1}x\) and \(dv=\sin x\,dx\). Then \(du=(n-1)\sin^{n-2}x\cos x\,dx\) and \(v=-\cos x\).
So
\[I_n=-\sin^{n-1}x\cos x+(n-1)\int \sin^{n-2}x\cos^2x\,dx.\]
Use \(\cos^2x=1-\sin^2x\):
\[I_n=-\sin^{n-1}x\cos x+(n-1)I_{n-2}-(n-1)I_n.\]
Thus
\[nI_n=-\sin^{n-1}x\cos x+(n-1)I_{n-2}.\]
Therefore
\[\boxed{I_n=-\frac{\sin^{n-1}x\cos x}{n}+\frac{n-1}{n}I_{n-2}}.\]

Use
\[\sin x\cos x=\frac12\sin2x.\]
Then
\[\sin^2x\cos^2x=\frac14\sin^2 2x.\]
Apply \(\sin^2 y=\frac{1-\cos2y}{2}\) with \(y=2x\):
\[\frac14\sin^2 2x=\frac18(1-\cos4x).\]
Integrate:
\[\int \sin^2x\cos^2x\,dx=\frac18\int(1-\cos4x)dx.\]
Therefore
\[\boxed{\frac{x}{8}-\frac{\sin4x}{32}+C}.\]
